h1: The 6 Best Pressure Cookers Under $100 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Pressure Cookers Under $100: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six pressure cookers under $100, from 6-quart multi-cookers to a stovetop pot, compared on size, functions and pot material.
summary: The Cosori 6QT 9-in-1 is the best pressure cooker under $100, an electric multi-cooker with a ceramic-coated pot and twelve listed safety features. The Instant Pot Duo Plus has a stainless steel pot and extra presets, and the RIO Mini and Duo Mini suit smaller households. The OLIXIS is the cheapest electric model, and the Hawkins Contura is a stovetop pot.
intro: Shoppers under $100 tend to assume capacity separates one pressure cooker from another, and the box encourages the belief. It does not do most of the work. The inner pot material decides how the pot ages, whether it is electric or stovetop decides how much attention it demands, and the safety features decide whether first-time use feels calm or nervous. Capacity only matters once those three are settled.

Our editors reviewed six pressure cookers by their spec pages and ranked them on the Primea score, weighting capacity, inner pot, function count and listed safety features. Prices are buckets only. Four are electric multi-cookers and one is a stovetop pot, and the listings leave out pressure ratings, so we do not compare them on power.

products.name: Cosori Pressure Cooker 6QT, 9-in-1, Ceramic Coating Pot, 12 Safety Features
products.verdict: A 6-quart, 9-in-1 electric cooker with the most listed safety features.
products.description:
The Cosori is a 6-quart electric pressure cooker that bundles nine functions and lists twelve safety features. Its inner pot has a ceramic coating, in the $50 to $100 bucket. A coating makes cleanup easy, and a long safety list matters because lid locks and release valves are the parts that keep pressure cooking uneventful.

It ranks first because it delivers full family capacity and the widest function range at the lowest 6-quart price, and its safety list is the longest here. The Duo Plus beats it on pot material but costs more.

Buy it for families wanting one capable multi-cooker on a budget. The caveats are that a coated pot can wear and the brand is less known than Instant Pot. Skip it if you want a stainless steel inner pot.
products.idealFor: Families wanting one capable multi-cooker on a budget.
products.skipIf: You want a stainless steel inner pot.

products.name: Instant Pot Duo Plus 6-Qt 9-in-1 Electric Pressure Cooker, Stainless Steel
products.verdict: A 6-quart, 9-in-1 with a stainless steel pot and extra presets.
products.description:
The Duo Plus is a 6-quart electric cooker with nine functions and a stainless steel inner pot. It adds more presets than the base Duo, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Stainless does not chip or flake, so it survives years of scrubbing, and presets save you from guessing times for rice or beans.

It ranks second because a stainless pot lasts longer than a coating and the presets save guesswork, but it sits closer to the $100 ceiling and costs more than the Cosori. The capacity and function count match.

Buy it for buyers who want a durable steel pot and a trusted brand. The caveats are the price near the ceiling and the extra cost over the Cosori. Skip it if you need to stay well below $100.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a durable steel pot.
products.skipIf: You need to stay well below $100.

products.name: Instant Pot 4QT RIO Mini 7-in-1 Multi-Cooker, Pressure Cooker, Slow cook, Sauté, Steam, Rice Maker, Yogurt, & Warmer
products.verdict: A 4-quart Instant Pot that suits small families at a lower price.
products.description:
The RIO Mini is a 4-quart, 7-in-1 multi-cooker from Instant Pot in a black finish. It covers pressure cooking, slow cooking, sautéing, steaming, rice, yogurt and warming, in the $50 to $100 bucket. Four quarts holds a family dinner for two to three people with leftovers.

It ranks third because 4 quarts is the sweet spot for small households, though it has fewer functions than the Cosori and costs nearly as much as the 6-quart models. Against the Duo Mini, it adds a quart.

Buy it for couples and small families. The caveats are limited batch size and fewer functions. Skip it if you batch cook for a crowd.
products.skipIf: You batch cook for a crowd.

products.name: Instant Pot Duo 7-in-1 Mini Electric Pressure Cooker, Slow Rice Cooker, Steamer, Sauté, Yogurt Maker, Warmer & Sterilizer
products.verdict: A 3-quart electric cooker with a companion app for recipes.
products.description:
The Duo Mini is a 3-quart stainless steel electric cooker that does seven jobs and pairs with a companion app of recipes, in the $50 to $100 bucket. A small pot heats quickly and stores easily, which suits a small kitchen.

It ranks fourth because 3 quarts is tight next to the 4-quart RIO Mini. The app and the Instant Pot name keep it competitive, and the stainless pot is a plus over coated rivals.

Buy it for singles, couples and small kitchens. The caveats are the small capacity and being smaller than the RIO Mini. Skip it if you regularly cook for four or more.
products.skipIf: You regularly cook for four or more.

products.name: OLIXIS 10-In-1 Electric Pressure Cooker, 3 Quart Multi Cooker for Rice, Stew and Steam, Small Programmable Stainless Steel
products.verdict: The cheapest programmable electric option, with ten functions.
products.description:
The OLIXIS is a 3-quart electric cooker with ten functions, programmable controls and a ceramic inner pot, priced in the $25 to $50 bucket. Ten modes at this price are a lot, though the count matters less than the quality behind it.

It ranks fifth because the brand is little known next to Instant Pot and Cosori, though it is the cheapest electric model here. A ceramic pot offers easy cleanup but wears like any coating.

Buy it for first-time buyers on a tight budget. The caveats are the unknown brand and the small capacity. Skip it if you want a proven brand.
products.idealFor: First-time buyers on a tight budget.

products.name: Hawkins 3 Litre Contura Black Pressure Cooker, Hard Anodised Inner Lid Cooker, Handi Cooker, Black (CB30)
products.verdict: A 3-liter hard-anodized stovetop cooker with no electronics.
products.description:
The Hawkins Contura is a 3-liter stovetop pressure cooker made of hard-anodized metal with an inner-lid design. It uses no electricity, in the $25 to $50 bucket. Hard-anodized aluminum is tough and conducts heat evenly, and an inner lid seals under pressure.

It ranks last only because it lacks the multi-function convenience of the electric models. You must watch the stove and judge pressure, which suits cooks used to the method.

Buy it for traditional cooks who like a stovetop pot. The caveats are manual monitoring and a single purpose. Skip it if you want a hands-off multi-cooker.
products.idealFor: Traditional cooks who like a stovetop pot.

whatMatters.detail: Capacity is measured in quarts or liters and sets how much you can cook at once. 3 quarts feeds one to three people, 6 quarts feeds a family. Check the quart figure in the title and avoid a pot you cannot fill to the right level, since most cookers should not be run nearly empty or past the max line. Overfilling is the leading cause of messy venting.

Electric multi-cookers regulate pressure and time for you, while stovetop pots need monitoring but are simple. Check whether the listing says electric or stovetop and match it to how you cook. Electric suits hands-off cooking, and stovetop suits cooks who like control and fewer parts that can fail. Know which style you will actually use.

Stainless steel is durable, ceramic coatings are nonstick but can wear, and hard-anodized metal is tough. Look for the material in the bullets and consider how you clean. A coated pot needs gentle tools, while stainless forgives scrubbing but can stick on rice or eggs. A small amount of oil usually solves it.

A 9-in-1 or 10-in-1 label covers modes such as rice, sauté and yogurt. More modes help only if you use them. Read which functions are named rather than the count alone, and favor a pot with solid pressure cooking and sauté, since those are the two jobs most cooks rely on. Ignore modes you will never touch.

Pressure cookers should have lid locks and pressure release systems. The Cosori lists twelve. Check for safety features in the listing and read the manual before first use, and do a water test to learn how the lid seals before cooking real food.

faq.q: Is a 6-quart pressure cooker too big for two people?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but it uses more counter space and stores awkwardly. A 3 or 4 quart model like the RIO Mini is easier for a couple, and it stores in a smaller cupboard. A big cooker for two often sits unused.

faq.q: What mistake do first-time buyers make?
faq.a: Overfilling. Most cookers have a maximum fill line, and ignoring it risks blockages and mess, especially with foods that foam like beans and rice. Fill to half for those.

faq.q: Is the Duo Plus worth it over the Cosori?
faq.a: If you want stainless steel and more presets, yes. Otherwise the Cosori offers similar capacity for less. The extra presets save guesswork, nothing more.

Read the manual, do a water test, and learn the pressure release method before cooking real food, because a dry run reveals leaks. The Cosori's safety features help, but practice builds confidence. Never force a stuck lid open.

faq.q: How do I look after a ceramic-coated pot?
faq.a: Wash gently by hand, use non-metal utensils, and avoid abrasive scrubbers to protect the coating, and replace a pot whose coating flakes. The same care applies to the OLIXIS ceramic pot, and to any coated liner. Replace the pot if the coating flakes.

faq.q: Can I use a stovetop cooker on induction?
faq.a: Check the base, because stovetop pots need a flat, compatible bottom. The Hawkins listing does not mention induction, so confirm compatibility before buying for an induction hob. Aluminum bases often need a magnetic plate.

finalTake: Buy the Cosori for a family that wants one capable cooker for the money, and the Duo Plus if you prefer a stainless steel pot. The RIO Mini and Duo Mini fit couples and small kitchens, while the OLIXIS is the lowest-cost electric option. Choose the Hawkins only if you like stovetop cooking. Read the manual and do a water test before first use.
